title: Bridge and Regiment
premise: In the winter of 1899, during a colonial border war, Felix Lockridge tends wounded soldiers in a requisitioned river town and secretly records in his ledger the names of civilians and conscripts erased from official reports. When Colonel Ashworth's men seize the town's records to bury evidence of a massacre at Marrow Bridge, Felix realizes his ledger is the last honest account in existence. Aided by Ada Quill, a telegraph operator with her own debts, he smuggles the ledger past three checkpoints toward a journalist waiting across the river, discovering that survival bought with silence is its own kind of death. The book ends at midnight on New Year's Eve: Felix delivers the names, refuses a pardon that would require recanting, and chooses exile over erasure, while Ada sends one final transmission that makes the massacre impossible to deny.
about_author: Yara Galloway is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing military correspondence from forgotten colonial campaigns. She writes historical fiction about the people history files under 'miscellaneous.'

chapters.title: The Ledger of Small Names
chapters.summary: Felix Lockridge, POV. In a converted schoolhouse infirmary, Felix treats feverish conscripts and records in his private ledger the dead the officers' reports omit—a farm boy here, a drowned porter there. He tells himself he is only a nurse, that history happens elsewhere. Emotional beat: quiet complicity masked as humility.

chapters.title: Requisition
chapters.summary: Felix, POV. Soldiers in new gray uniforms occupy the town, billeting in homes and converting the telegraph office to army use. Felix watches Mrs. Halloway evicted from her own kitchen and writes her name in the ledger. Emotional beat: the first crack in his belief that invisibility protects anyone.

chapters.title: The Operator
chapters.summary: Ada Quill, POV. Ada works the army telegraph, transcribing dispatches she knows are lies—casualty figures halved, engagements invented. She notices Felix's careful handwriting on supply forms and suspects he keeps accounts of his own. Emotional beat: wary recognition between two people fluent in official falsehood.

chapters.title: Marrow Bridge
chapters.summary: Felix, POV. Wounded survivors of an engagement at Marrow Bridge arrive delirious, describing the shooting of surrendered villagers. Felix treats them and writes eleven names into the ledger, hands shaking. An officer orders the men's testimony 'not recorded.' Emotional beat: horror arriving not as spectacle but as paperwork.

chapters.title: Colonel Ashworth's Clean War
chapters.summary: Ashworth, POV. The colonel drafts his report of Marrow Bridge: a legitimate action against armed irregulars, zero civilian casualties. He orders all town records consolidated for transport to headquarters—sanitized or destroyed. Emotional beat: chilling sincerity; he believes he is protecting the empire from itself.

chapters.title: What the Army Takes
chapters.summary: Felix, POV. Soldiers cart away parish registers, merchant ledgers, the school's roll books. Felix hides his own ledger inside a crate of surgical dressings, realizing too late that hiding it marks him as guilty if found. Emotional beat: fear sharpening into resolve.

chapters.title: A Debt in Copper Wire
chapters.summary: Ada, POV. Ada reveals why she cooperates: her brother was executed for desertion after a trial lasting nine minutes, and she has been transmitting the army's version ever since. She offers Felix something better than hiding the ledger—sending it, name by name, in cipher through the wire. Emotional beat: guilt finding a purpose.

chapters.title: Cipher and Candlelight
chapters.summary: Alternating POVs. Over three nights, Ada encodes the ledger's names into weather reports and freight manifests while Felix stands watch, inventing plausible traffic. They grow close over shared cigarettes and shared silences. Emotional beat: intimacy built from conspiracy.

chapters.title: Sergeant Bray Counts Heads
chapters.summary: Bray, POV. The checkpoint sergeant, no fool, notices the telegraph traffic doubled since the occupation and begins keeping his own private tally of anomalies. He doesn't know what the pattern means yet—but patterns are his trade. Emotional beat: the hunter assembling without knowing it.

chapters.title: The First Checkpoint
chapters.summary: Felix, POV. Ordered to escort medical supplies across the river, Felix carries the physical ledger sewn into a stretcher canvas. At the bridge checkpoint Bray searches the convoy slowly, enjoying his power. Felix passes by inches when a dying soldier's hemorrhage forces an urgent crossing. Emotional beat: terror braided with shame at using a patient as cover.

chapters.title: The Man Across the River
chapters.summary: Ada, POV. Ada confirms the recipient: Elias Voss, a disgraced correspondent camped in a fishing village, the only journalist willing to print what the war office denies. But her transmission requesting contact is intercepted and flagged by Ashworth's signals officer. Emotional beat: hope shadowed by the closing net.

chapters.title: Interrogation by Courtesy
chapters.summary: Ashworth, POV. Ashworth invites Felix to dinner, courteous and lethal, asking about his 'private notes' and offering promotion in exchange for loyalty. Felix understands the offer is a test and declines carefully. Emotional beat: the seduction of complicity resisted by a thread.

chapters.title: Burn Notice
chapters.summary: Felix, POV. Ashworth orders the infirmary's stores burned as a typhus precaution—including the crate where the ledger once hid. Felix learns the copy Ada transmitted covers only half the names; the rest exist only in his memory and the stretcher canvas already across the river. Emotional beat: the cost of half-measures made brutal.

chapters.title: The Second Checkpoint
chapters.summary: Alternating POVs. Ada must physically carry the remaining names as encoded punch-tapes disguised as repair spools. Bray, now suspicious, detains her at the ferry landing and reads her manifest aloud. She bluffs with genuine technical authority—and a forged order Felix risked everything to produce. Emotional beat: nerve stretched to snapping.

chapters.title: Betrayal at the Boathouse
chapters.summary: Felix, POV. Corporal Dunn, a wounded man Felix saved, trades information for his mother's evacuation papers, revealing the telegraph conspiracy. Ada is arrested; Felix escapes through the marsh because Dunn hesitates one crucial second. Emotional beat: gratitude curdling—the price of survival paid in someone else's blood.

chapters.title: Cells and Ciphers
chapters.summary: Ada, POV. Interrogated by Ashworth, Ada gives up nothing but performs confession, feeding him a false cipher key that will garble his own intercepts. Alone in her cell, she recites the names she memorized like prayers. Emotional beat: resistance as endurance rather than heroics.

chapters.title: The Third Checkpoint
chapters.summary: Felix, POV. The final crossing at Marrow Bridge itself, now fortified for New Year's Eve. Felix joins a column of evacuated wounded, carrying the last names tattooed nowhere but in his head and a scrap hidden in his boot. Bray stops him, recognizes him, and—having read enough intercepted truth to doubt his own side—lets him pass, deserting his post. Emotional beat: justice outside the law, chosen by an unlikely hand.

chapters.title: Midnight Deadline
chapters.summary: Felix, POV. In Voss's freezing fishing hut, Felix dictates the final names as Voss sets type by lamplight, the century expiring around them. Church bells, gunfire, the press clanking. Ashworth's pardon offer arrives by rider: freedom for silence. Emotional beat: climax as choice—the ledger finished or the life preserved, not both.

chapters.title: The Refusal
chapters.summary: Felix, POV. Felix sends back the pardon unsigned with a single line: 'History happened here.' The first printed sheets go out with the dawn tide. Ashworth, reading the newspaper in his headquarters, understands the war's story has slipped his grasp forever. Emotional beat: the quiet thunder of consequences beginning.

chapters.title: What Ada Sent
chapters.summary: Ada, POV. Released when the scandal breaks, Ada transmits one final uncoded message on the open band: every name, every date, repeated until the army cuts her wire. Townsfolk gather in the snow to listen. Emotional beat: grief transfigured into public memory.

chapters.title: Exile's Arithmetic
chapters.summary: Felix, POV. Unable to return under amnesty terms requiring recantation, Felix boards a ship with Voss, tallying what survival cost: Dunn's betrayal, Bray's ruin, Ada left behind. He starts a new ledger—not of the dead, but of the living who helped. Emotional beat: mourning and gratitude balanced in the same hand.

chapters.title: Bridge and Regiment
chapters.summary: Ada, POV, epilogue. Years later, Ada receives a parcel: Felix's new ledger, its first page bearing her name, and a newspaper clipping of the Marrow Bridge inquiry reopening. She walks to the rebuilt bridge at dusk and speaks the names aloud to the water. Emotional beat: resolution as remembrance—truth outlives the regimes that buried it.
